## [Emission standards]{.en}[排放标准]{.zh}

::: {.en}
**Table C1. Daily emission limits and Wanxing readings (mg/Nm³, 11% O₂, dry)**

::: tw
  Pollutant              GB 18485-2014 daily   EU IED daily   EU BAT-AEL, new plants   Wanxing, 14 Oct 2026
  ---------------------- --------------------- -------------- ------------------------ -------------------------
  Dust                   20                    10             \<2–5                    0.264
  NOx                    250                   200            50–120                   76.29
  SO₂                    80                    50             5–30                     14.37
  HCl                    50                    10             \<2–6                    1.961
  CO                     80                    50             10–50                    5.824
  Mercury                0.05                  0.05           0.005–0.02               not published daily
  Dioxins (ng TEQ/Nm³)   0.1                   0.1            \<0.01–0.04              periodic tests; request
:::

*Sources: \[23, 118–120\]. Wanxing values are furnace 1 daily averages for one day, taken from the public platform. They are a snapshot until the full hourly and annual series is available. EU limits are a benchmark here, not a Victorian legal limit \[46\].*

![](../assets/img/christine-fig11.jpg\){fig-alt="Wanxing daily averages as a share of EU daily limits"}

*Figure C1. Wanxing daily averages as a share of EU daily limits (one day, furnace 1).*

**Why moisture and heating value matter.** Wet food waste lowers the usable heat per kilogram, because energy is spent evaporating water. A furnace is designed to burn waste steadily and completely, recover heat, limit pollutants, and avoid corrosion and slagging. Heating value is a key design input, but not the only one. In Victoria the issue reverses: drier, richer residual waste (3.3) can push a grate towards its thermal limit.
:::
